# Short answer

For most full-size fridges, get a **pure sine wave station with at least ~1,300 W of surge and about 1,500-2,000 Wh of capacity** to cover a full 24 hours. About 1,000 Wh covers roughly half a day to a day.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Surge watts:** A compressor spikes when it starts, commonly 1,000-2,400 W on a household fridge. Sources suggest planning for at least 1,200-1,300 W of surge. This is the spec that most often trips small units, even when their capacity is large ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
2. **Continuous watts:** A fridge runs at about 100-250 W while the compressor is on, so almost any 1,000 W-class station clears this.
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time. One test case, an 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR fridge, averages about 41 W, or roughly 1,000 Wh/day. With inverter losses and 20% headroom, that's about **1,400 Wh per day** ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). Other sources estimate higher averages (50-70 W), so the 1,500-2,000 Wh range for a full day is safer.

Choose a pure sine wave inverter. Modified sine wave can make compressors run hot or fail to start.

## Find your own number
Look at your fridge's EnergyGuide label: **kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 = average watts**. Multiply by the hours you need, divide by ~0.85 for inverter losses, and add ~20% margin. A big side-by-side with an ice maker can average about twice the ENERGY STAR figure, while a small fridge averages about half. Keeping the door shut helps a lot.

## Sizing guide and picks

| Outage length | Capacity | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Up to ~12-17 hours | ~1,000-1,150 Wh | [BLUETTI AC180](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180) (1,152 Wh, 2,700 W surge, $499) |
| ~1 day | ~1,500-2,100 Wh | [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2) (2,073 Wh, $899) |
| 1 day, expandable later | 2,048 Wh, expandable to 8,192 Wh | [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) ($899) |
| 2+ days | ~3,000 Wh | [BLUETTI Elite 300](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-300) (3,014 Wh, $1,199, was on pre-order as of Oct 24) |

- The [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) (1,070 Wh, about $499) is a similar option to the AC180. HomeGridHQ estimates about 17 hours for a typical fridge. That page doesn't give a direct buy link.
- The [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak) is another 2 kWh-class option.

The BLUETTI links above are affiliate links, and the retailer is paid if you buy. The BLUETTI AC180 and Elite 200 V2 prices come from the dealectric.com listings (checked Oct 21-24), and the Jackery price from HomeGridHQ. Prices move.

## Things to avoid
Units under ~600 W of output or ~300 Wh, such as the Tenergy T320 and ALLPOWERS R600, are built for phones, laptops, and CPAP. They can't start or sustain a fridge ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/answers/how-much-power-does-a-household-refrigerator-use-watts-startup-surge-energy-per-)).

If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year and how long an outage you want to cover, I can narrow this to one pick.
